Instability results for the wave equation in the interior of Kerr black holes

Jonathan Luk Thanks: jluk@dpmms.cam.ac.uk    Jan Sbierski Thanks: jjs48@cam.ac.uk
August 8, 2026
Abstract

We prove that a large class of smooth solutions ψ\psi to the linear wave equation □g​ψ=0\Box_{g}\psi=0 on subextremal rotating Kerr spacetimes which are regular and decaying along the event horizon become singular at the Cauchy horizon. More precisely, we show that assuming appropriate upper and lower bounds on the energy along the event horizon, the solution has infinite (non-degenerate) energy on any spacelike hypersurfaces intersecting the Cauchy horizon transversally. Extrapolating from known results in the Reissner–Nordström case, the assumed upper and lower bounds required for our theorem are conjectured to hold for solutions arising from generic smooth and compactly supported initial data on a Cauchy hypersurface. This result is motivated by the strong cosmic censorship conjecture in general relativity.

1 Introduction

In this paper, we study the linear instability of the Kerr Cauchy horizon under scalar perturbations. More precisely, we consider the linear wave equation11 1 Here, □g\Box_{g} denotes the standard Laplace–Beltrami operator for the Kerr metric gg. on the black hole interior of subextremal Kerr spacetime with non-vanishing angular momentum (i.e., for Kerr parameters 0<|a|<M0<|a|<M - see (2.1) for the formula for the metric)

(1.1) □g​ψ=0\Box_{g}\psi=0

with (characteristic) initial data posed on the event horizon. We prove that there exists a large class of smooth, polynomially decaying22 2 with respect to the function v+v_{+} (see Section 2). data such that the solutions have infinite non-degenerate energy on any spacelike hypersurface intersecting the Cauchy horizon transversally. In particular, such solutions do not belong to Wl​o​c1,2W^{1,2}_{loc} in any neighbourhood of any point on the Cauchy horizon. In addition to merely constructing singular solutions, our main theorem identifies a sufficient condition only in terms of upper and lower bounds of appropriate energy along the event horizon that guarantees the solution blows up at the Cauchy horizon. We state our main result roughly as follows and refer the readers to Theorem 3.2 for a precise statement.

Theorem 1.2 (Rough version of main theorem).

Let ψ\psi be a smooth solution to (1.1) in the interior of a subextremal Kerr spacetime with non-vanishing angular momentum. If the energy of ψ\psi along the event horizon obeys some polynomial upper and lower bounds (see i)-iii) of Theorem 3.2 for precise bounds), then the non-degenerate energy33 3 See Remark 3.11 for further discussions on the non-degenerate energy. on any spacelike hypersurface intersecting the Cauchy horizon transversally is infinite.

Our result is motivated by the celebrated strong cosmic censorship conjecture in general relativity. We will not discuss this conjecture in detail, but refer the readers to [6, 7, 17] for further discussions. For the purpose of this paper, it suffices to say that the maximal globally hyperbolic development of the Kerr solution for 0<|a|<M0<|a|<M has a smooth Cauchy horizon and the strong cosmic censorship conjecture suggests the following instability conjecture of the Kerr Cauchy horizon for small perturbations of Kerr:

Conjecture 1.3.

Generic small perturbations of Kerr initial data for the Einstein vacuum equations

(1.4) R​i​c​(g)μ​ν=0Ric(g)_{\mu\nu}=0

lead to maximal globally hyperbolic developments such that the Cauchy horizons are so-called weak null singularities. In particular, for any continuous extensions of the spacetime metric, the spacetime Christoffel symbols are not square-integrable.

Early formulations of this instability conjecture often suggest an even stronger instability - namely, that a spacelike singularity may form “prior to the Cauchy horizon” and that the spacetime does not contain a Cauchy horizon at all. However, recent work [7] shows that the Kerr Cauchy horizon is in fact C0C^{0}-stable if one assumes that the exterior region of Kerr is stable is a reasonably strong sense. On the other hand, the estimates proven in [7] are consistent with the spacetime not having square integrable Christoffel symbols. One can therefore still hope that the weaker formulation of the instability conjecture based on the non-square-integrability of Christoffel symbols may hold.44 4 This formulation is due to Christodoulou [3]. In particular, if this formulation of the conjecture holds, then the maximal globally hyperbolic developments of generic initial data in a small neighbourhood of Kerr data admit no extensions as weak solutions to the Einstein vacuum equations.

Theorem 1.2 can be viewed as a first step towards establishing Conjecture 1.3. Instead of considering the full nonlinear Einstein vacuum equations, we only study a much simpler model equation, namely the linear scalar wave equation (1.1). This can be regarded as a simplified linearization of the Einstein equations in which we ignore the tensorial structure of the system and drop all the lower order terms55 5 Notice in particular that the linear equation that we study is not a true linearization of the Einstein vacuum equations.. We prove in Theorem 1.2 that at least in this much simpler setting, there is indeed an instability mechanism. If one moreover naively compares66 6 Recall that in a generalized wave coordinate system, (1.4) becomes a wave equation for the metric gg. We should remark however that this comparison is best taken only at a heuristic level, as a resolution of Conjecture 1.3 will likely not be based on generalized wave coordinates (cf. [7]). the metric in (1.4) with the scalar field in (1.1), then the infinitude of the non-degenerate energy of ψ\psi corresponds to the blow-up of the Ll​o​c2L^{2}_{loc} norm of the Christoffel symbols as in Conjecture 1.3.

There is a long tradition in both mathematics and physics in studying the linear scalar wave equation on black hole backgrounds. The existence of solutions to the linear wave equation on Kerr which are regular at the event horizon but singular at the Cauchy horizon have been previously constructed in [20, 23] (see also [12]). Therefore, the main novelty of Theorem 1.2 is that it gives a sufficient condition for the solution to be singular at the Cauchy horizon only in terms of L2L^{2} upper and lower bounds of the solution along the event horizon. Moreover, motivated by the known results in the case of the subextremal Reissner--Nordström spacetime77 7 See Section 1.2 for the metric of Reissner–Nordström spacetime and discussions on its geometry.88 8 One can view the subextremal Reissner–Nordström spacetime (with non-vanishing charge) as a “poor-man’s version” of the subextremal Kerr spacetime (with non-vanishing angular momentum) in the sense that they have similar global geometries, including having smooth Cauchy horizons, while the geometry in the Reissner–Nordström case is simpler. Indeed, as we will discuss in Section 1.1, more is known about solutions to the linear wave equation in Reissner–Nordström. Moreover, in that case, there exists solutions arising from smooth and compactly supported Cauchy data such that analogues of the assumptions of Theorem 1.2 hold (see Section 1.1). with non-vanishing charge, one may conjecture that the bounds that are needed in the assumptions of Theorem 1.2 hold for some solutions to the linear wave equation arising from smooth and compactly supported initial data on a complete 2-ended Cauchy hypersurface. This conjecture, if true, means that generic smooth and compactly supported initial data on a Cauchy hypersurface lead to solutions that are singular at the Cauchy horizon. We will return to this point in the discussions in Section 1.1.

Our proof of Theorem 1.2 is based on energy identities and energy estimates in the interior of the Kerr black hole, which are established by appropriate choices of various vector fields. Most importantly, we rely on the conservation law99 9 Recall Noether’s theorem which allows us to obtain a conservation law for the solutions to a wave equation from a symmetry of the underlying spacetime. associated to a Killing vector field T𝒞​ℋ+T_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}} (see (3.1) for the definition) which extends the null generators of the Cauchy horizon. This conservation law lets us propagate an L2L^{2} lower bound from the event horizon up to a spacelike hypersurface γσ\gamma_{\sigma} (see (2.4) for the definition) that approaches the Cauchy horizon “at timelike infinity”. For an appropriate choice of the hypersurface γσ\gamma_{\sigma}, we can then propagate this lower bound to a hypersurface transversally intersecting the Cauchy horizon using the energy identity associated to the (non-Killing!) vector field Δρ2∂r+r2+a2ρ2∂t+aρ2∂φ\frac{\Delta}{\rho^{2}}\partial_{r}+\frac{r^{2}+a^{2}}{\rho^{2}}\partial_{t}+\frac{a}{\rho^{2}}\partial_{\varphi}. In order to1010 10 In fact, stability estimates are also needed to bound the “boundary terms” in the conservation law associated to T𝒞​ℋ+T_{\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}} (see discussions in Section 1.2). control the error terms arising from this energy identity, we need to prove sufficiently strong stability estimates, which in turn are also obtained via energy estimates. We refer the readers to further discussions on the ideas of the proof in Section 1.2 where we sketch the argument in the slightly simpler case of the Reissner–Nordström spacetime.

In the remainder of the introduction, we will discuss the global Cauchy problem for (1.1) in Section 1.1. In particular, we will point out the relevance of Theorem 1.2 to the global Cauchy problem. Then, in Section 1.2, we will outline some ideas of the proof in the setting of the Reissner–Nordström spacetime. Finally, we will end the introduction with an outline of the remainder of the paper.

1.1 The global Cauchy problem

With an eye towards the instability of Kerr Cauchy horizon conjecture (Conjecture 1.3), one would like to go beyond the study of solutions to the linear wave equation within the interior of the black hole region as in Theorem 1.2, but instead consider the problem of global evolution, where the initial data are prescribed on a 22-ended complete asymptotically flat Cauchy hypersurface Σ0\Sigma_{0} (see1111 11 Here, the interior of black hole region depicted in Figure 2 on page 2 should be thought of as the top “diamond” region in Figure 1. Figure 1).

Due to the blue-shift effect associated with the Cauchy horizon, it has been expected since the pioneering work of Simpson–Penrose [24] that there is a global instability for the Cauchy problem such that generic regular data give rise to solutions which are singular at the Cauchy horizon. This problem has been widely studied in the physics literature, see for instance [2, 16, 18, 19].

The first rigorous result on the instability of solutions to the linear wave equation dates back to McNamara [20], who gave a conditional1212 12 Notice that in the case of Reissner-Nordström, the condition also was shown to hold in [20]. proof of the existence of solutions arising from regular polynomially decaying data but are singular at the Cauchy horizon, subject to verifying a condition regarding the non-triviality of the “scattering map” of the solutions from past null infinity to the the Cauchy horizon. This condition has recently been proven by Dafermos–Shlapentokh-Rothman [12], who also gave an alternative proof of this result as part of their general treatment of blue-shift instabilities on black hole spacetimes. We give a rough version of the theorem here and refer the readers to [12] for a precise statement:

Theorem 1.5 (McNamara [20], Dafermos–Shlapentokh-Rothman [12]).

On any subextremal Kerr spacetime with non-vanishing angular momentum, there exist solutions to the linear wave equation which arise from polynomially decaying data (with an arbitrarily fast polynomial rate) on past null infinity but are singular at the Cauchy horizon.

Another construction of solutions which are singular at the Cauchy horizon but have finite initial energy follows from the results of Sbierski. More precisely, the following was proven in [23] by geometric optics considerations:

Theorem 1.6 (Sbierski [23]).

Consider a subextremal Kerr spacetime with non-vanishing angular momentum. Let Σ0\Sigma_{0} be a complete 22-ended asymptotically flat Cauchy hypersurface and Σ1\Sigma_{1} be a spacelike hypersurface in the interior of the black hole intersecting the Cauchy horizon transversally (see Figure 1). There exists a sequence of solutions {ψi}i=1∞\{\psi_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\infty} to the linear wave equation □g​ψi=0\Box_{g}\psi_{i}=0 such that the initial energies on Σ0\Sigma_{0} satisfy E⁡(ψi,Σ0)=1E(\psi_{i},\Sigma_{0})=1 while the non-degenerate energies on Σ1\Sigma_{1} obey E⁡(ψi,Σ1)→+∞E(\psi_{i},\Sigma_{1})\to+\infty.

Given the above result, an application of the closed graph theorem1313 13 More precisely, we use the following consequence of the closed graph theorem: Let XX, YY, ZZ be Banach spaces and T:X→YT:X\to Y, Q:Y→ZQ:Y\to Z be linear maps. If QQ is bounded and injective and Q∘TQ\circ T is bounded, then TT is bounded. In our setting, let XX be the energy space on Σ0\Sigma_{0}, YY and ZZ be the non-degenerate and degenerate energy spaces on Σ1\Sigma_{1} respectively. If for the sake of argument that all solutions initially in the energy class on Σ0\Sigma_{0} belong to the non-degnerate energy class on Σ1\Sigma_{1}, then we can define TT to be the operator “solving the wave equation” and QQ to be the inclusion map and derive a contradiction with Theorem 1.6 using the above functional analytic statement. The key remaining analytic ingredient is the boundedness of Q∘TQ\circ T, i.e., the boundedness of the degenerate energy, which follows from [11] together with considerations in Section 4. implies the existence of solutions which initially belong to the energy class but then fail to be in the non-degenerate energy class near the Cauchy horizon.

In the constructions in Theorems 1.5 and 1.6 above, the solutions do not have compact support on the Cauchy hypersurface Σ0\Sigma_{0}. As pointed out in [23], Theorem 1.6 also holds in the extremal case, i.e., when 0<|a|=M0<|a|=M. In that case, however, the instability may in fact be milder - it is known that for axisymmetric data on extremal Kerr spacetimes which decay sufficiently fast on a Cauchy hypersurface1414 14 By saying this, we have chosen a globally hyperbolic subset of the extremal Kerr spacetime for which there is an (incomplete!) asymptotically flat Cauchy hypersurface which extends into the black hole region. For precise statements, see [23, 15]., the corresponding solutions to the linear wave equation have finite non-degenerate energy in the interior of the black hole [15] (see also [14, 22]). In other words, the analogue of Theorem 1.6 in the extremal case only holds because one considers general Cauchy data in the energy class. On the other hand, in the case of subextremal Kerr spacetime, it is indeed expected that the singularity at the Cauchy horizon is not an artefact of the slow decay of the initial data at spacelike infinity. It is therefore desirable to obtain an instability result for smooth and compactly supported Cauchy data. We formulate this as a conjecture:

Conjecture 1.7.

Generic smooth and compactly supported Cauchy data on Σ0\Sigma_{0} to the linear wave equation (1.1) in subextremal rotating Kerr spacetimes give rise to solutions such that the non-degenerate energy on any spacelike hypersurface intersecting the Cauchy horizon transversally is infinite.

While the above conjecture remains an open problem, an analogue in the Reissner–Nordström spacetime has been recently established:

Theorem 1.8 (Luk–Oh [17]).

Given any Reissner–Nordström spacetime with 0<|e|<M0<|e|<M, generic smooth and compactly supported initial data on a complete 22-ended asymptotically flat Cauchy hypersurface Σ0\Sigma_{0} (Figure1515 15 Figure 1 was of course meant to depict the Kerr spacetime. However, since Kerr spacetime (for 0<|a|<M0<|a|<M) and Reissner–Nordström spacetime (for 0<|e|<M0<|e|<M) can be described by the same Penrose diagram, we also use it to depict the Reissner–Nordström spacetime for the purpose of the statement of this theorem. 1) give rise to solutions to the linear wave equation such that the non-degenerate energy on any spacelike hypersurface intersecting the Cauchy horizon transversally is infinite.

This theorem was proved in [17] via first showing that a lower bound1616 16 Although it was not explicitly used in [17], upper bounds analogous to those in Assumptions i) and iii) in Theorem 3.2 are also known in the Reissner-Nordström setting [8, 21, 25]. on the energy along the event horizon holds for a generic class of solutions arising from smooth and compactly supported data on Σ0\Sigma_{0}. This lower bound is in a similar form as that required for our main theorem (see assumption ii) of Theorem 3.2). Based on the known results in the Reissner–Nordström case, one can therefore hope that in the Kerr case, there exist smooth and compactly supported data on Σ0\Sigma_{0} such that the solutions obey the assumptions of Theorem 1.2 along the event horizon. In other words, by Theorem 1.2, Conjecture 1.7 can be reduced1717 17 Strictly speaking, the combination of Theorem 1.2 and Conjecture 1.9 only proves the existence of singular solutions arising from smooth and compactly supported initial data. Nevertheless, by virtue of the linearity of the wave equation, this would immediately implies the genericity of such singular solutions. to the following conjecture:

Conjecture 1.9.

There exist smooth and compactly supported initial data on a complete 22-ended asymptotically flat Cauchy hypersurface Σ0\Sigma_{0} (Figure 1) in Kerr spacetime (with 0<|a|<M0<|a|<M) such that the solutions to the linear wave equation (1.1) obey the assumptions on the energy along the event horizon in Theorem 1.2.

Let us finally remark that the upper bounds i) and iii) in the assumptions of Theorem 3.2 are known to hold for some q>0q>0 [9, 11, 21, 25]. Thus the main challenge is to obtain the lower bound ii). Moreover, one needs to show near optimal upper and lower bounds such that i) and ii) in the assumptions of Theorem 3.2 hold with the same q>0q>0.

1.2.1 Stability estimates

We now explain each of the steps above. The first step, i.e., the stability estimates, is already carried out in [13]. Since we need a slightly different version, we state it here in Proposition 1.14, with a brief sketch of the proof. The complete proof will be carried out in the Kerr case in Section 4, and in the sketch below, we will point out where the analogue of each of the steps in the Kerr case will be carried out in the paper.

Before we state the proposition on stability estimates, we first need to define a hypersurface in the interior of Reissner-Nordström, which plays a crucial role in the analysis. Define a function

fγσ​(v+,v−):=v++v−−σ​log⁡(v+)f_{\gamma_{\sigma}}(v_{+},v_{-}):=v_{+}+v_{-}-\sigma\log(v_{+})

for v+v_{+} sufficiently large and σ>0\sigma>0 and define a hypersurface γσ\gamma_{\sigma} in the interior of the Reissner–Nordström black hole by

An analogue of this hypersurface was first introduced by Dafermos [4, 5] in the setting of the Einstein–Maxwell–(real)–scalar–field system in spherical symmetry (see also [13]). This hypersurface has the important property that its future, restricted to the past of {v−=u0}\{v_{-}=u_{0}\} (for arbitrary u0u_{0}), has finite spacetime volume. This fact will be the underlying geometric reason that the error terms in Proposition 1.23 are under control.

The following are the main stability estimates:

1.2.2 Instability estimates

In the two steps of the instability estimates we deal with the regions to the past and to the future of γσ\gamma_{\sigma} respectively (recall the definition of γσ\gamma_{\sigma} in (1.13) and see Figure 6 for a depiction of the spacetime regions in the Kerr case). In the first step (see Proposition 1.21 below and Section 5.1 for the Kerr case), we use the conservation law associated to the vector field2323 23 In the Kerr case, we will use the conservation law associated to T𝒞​ℋ+T_{\mathcal{CH}^{+}}, see Section 5.1. ∂t\partial_{t} to prove a lower bound of the energy on γσ\gamma_{\sigma}. In the second step (see Proposition 1.23 below and Section 5.2 for the Kerr case), we then propagate the lower bound on γσ\gamma_{\sigma} to the {v−=u0}\{v_{-}=u_{0}\} hypersurface. In both of these steps, the stability estimates that have been derived play an important role.

Proposition 1.21.

There exists a sequence vk∈ℝv_{k}\in\mathbb{R} with vk→∞v_{k}\to\infty such that the following estimate holds on the hypersurface γσ{\gamma_{\sigma}}:

∫γσ∩{v+≥vk}𝕋(∂t,(−dfγσ)♯)volfγσ≳(vk)−(q+δ),\int\limits_{\gamma_{\sigma}\cap\{v_{+}\geq v_{k}\}}\mathbb{T}(\partial_{t},(-df_{\gamma_{\sigma}})^{\sharp})\,\mathrm{vol}_{f_{\gamma_{\sigma}}}\gtrsim(v_{k})^{-(q+\delta)},

where volfγσ\mathrm{vol}_{f_{\gamma_{\sigma}}} is chosen so that vol=d​fγσ∧volfγσ\mathrm{vol}=df_{\gamma_{\sigma}}\wedge\mathrm{vol}_{f_{\gamma_{\sigma}}}.

Sketch of proof.

We apply (1.12) with Z=∂tZ=\partial_{t}. Since ∂t\partial_{t} is Killing, we in fact obtain a conservation law, which implies the following lower bound for every vv:

(1.22) ∫γσ∩{v+≥v}𝕋(∂t,(−dfγσ)♯)volfγσ≳∫ℋ+∩{v+≥v}(∂v+ψ)2r2sin2θdv+dθdφ⏟=:I−C∫{v+=v}∩{fγσ≤1}((∂v−ψ)2+(−ΔR​N)|∇̸ψ|2)r2sin2θdv−dθdφ⏟=:I​I.\begin{split}&\int\limits_{\gamma_{\sigma}\cap\{v_{+}\geq v\}}\mathbb{T}(\partial_{t},(-df_{\gamma_{\sigma}})^{\sharp})\,\mathrm{vol}_{f_{\gamma_{\sigma}}}\\ \gtrsim&\underbrace{\int\limits_{\mathcal{H}^{+}\cap\{v_{+}\geq v\}}(\partial_{v_{+}}\psi)^{2}\,r^{2}\sin^{2}\theta\,dv_{+}\,d\theta\,d\varphi}_{=:I}\\ &-\underbrace{C\int\limits_{\{v_{+}=v\}\cap\{f_{\gamma_{\sigma}}\leq 1\}}\left((\partial_{v_{-}}\psi)^{2}+(-\Delta_{RN})|\not{\nabla}\psi|^{2}\right)\,r^{2}\sin^{2}\theta\,dv_{-}\,d\theta\,d\varphi}_{=:II}.\end{split}

Notice again that it is important that this is derived from a conservation law and there are no bulk terms. By assumption ii) of Theorem 1.10, the term II is bounded below by v−(q+δ)v^{-(q+\delta)}. To treat the terms II, we crucially rely on the stability estimate (1.15) which allows us to pick, using the pigeonhole principle, a sequence vk→∞v_{k}\to\infty as k→∞k\to\infty such that the corresponding term decays as (vk)−(q+1)+C​σ​(1−α)(v_{k})^{-(q+1)+C\sigma(1-\alpha)}. Since δ<1\delta<1, for every σ\sigma, one can choose α\alpha close to 11 to conclude the proof. ∎

Finally, we prove the main conclusion of Theorem 1.10:

Proposition 1.23.

For every u0∈ℝu_{0}\in\mathbb{R}, there exists a sequence vk∈ℝv_{k}\in\mathbb{R} with vk→∞v_{k}\to\infty as k→∞k\to\infty such that

∫{v−=u0}∩{v+≥vk}(∂v+ψ)2r2sin2θdvdθdφ≳(vk)−(q+δ).\int\limits_{\{v_{-}=u_{0}\}\cap\{v_{+}\geq v_{k}\}}(\partial_{v_{+}}\psi)^{2}r^{2}\sin^{2}\theta\,dv\,d\theta\,d\varphi\gtrsim(v_{k})^{-(q+\delta)}.

We use (1.12) with Z=∂v+Z=\partial_{v_{+}} in the region to the future of γσ\gamma_{\sigma} and to the past of {v−=u0}∪𝒞ℋ+\{v_{-}=u_{0}\}\cup\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+}. Noticing that the term ‘‘at the Cauchy horizon’’ vanishes2424 24 To justify this, one needs to use (1.15) and an approximation argument, see the proof of (5.9). and dropping a boundary term with a good sign, we have

First, II, which is the main term, can be bounded below by the term in Proposition 1.21. This is because ∂t=∂v+−∂v−\partial_{t}=\partial_{v_{+}}-\partial_{v_{-}} and the term ∫γσ∩{v+≥vk}𝕋(∂v−,(−dfγσ)♯)volfγσ\int\limits_{\gamma_{\sigma}\cap\{v_{+}\geq v_{k}\}}\mathbb{T}(\partial_{v_{-}},(-df_{\gamma_{\sigma}})^{\sharp})\,\mathrm{vol}_{f_{\gamma_{\sigma}}} has a favourable sign for this one-sided bound. Then, in order to control the bulk error term I​III in (1.24), the key observation is that by choosing σ>0\sigma>0 to be sufficiently large, the stability estimate (1.16) implies that I​III decays faster than any polynomial, i.e., for any pp, it is bounded by Cp​(vk)−pC_{p}(v_{k})^{-p}. The conclusion therefore follows by considering sufficiently large vkv_{k}. ∎

1.3 Outline of the paper

We end the introduction with an outline of the remainder of the paper. We will begin by a brief discussion on the geometry of the interior of the Kerr black hole in Section 2. We will also introduce the preliminaries about performing energy estimates in this section. We then give a precise statement of the main theorem in Section 3. The proof of the main theorem will then occupy the remainder of the paper: In Section 4, we prove the necessary stability estimates; in Section 5, we then prove the instability estimates, using in particular the bounds derived in Section 4.

2 The interior of subextremal Kerr spacetime

We consider the standard (t,r,θ,φ)(t,r,\theta,\varphi) coordinates on the smooth manifold ℳ=ℝ×(r−,r+)×𝕊2\mathcal{M}=\mathbb{R}\times(r_{-},r_{+})\times\mathbb{S}^{2}, where r−r_{-} and r+r_{+} will be defined momentarily. A Lorentzian metric gg on ℳ\mathcal{M} is defined by

(2.1) g=gt​t​d​t2+gt​φ​(d​t⊗d​φ+d​φ⊗d​t)+ρ2Δ​d​r2+ρ2​d​θ2+gφ​φ​d​φ2,g=g_{tt}\,dt^{2}+g_{t\varphi}\,(dt\otimes d\varphi+d\varphi\otimes dt)+\frac{\rho^{2}}{\Delta}\,dr^{2}+\rho^{2}\,d\theta^{2}+g_{\varphi\varphi}\,d\varphi^{2}\;,

where

ρ2=r2+a2cos2θ,\displaystyle\rho^{2}=r^{2}+a^{2}\cos^{2}\theta\;,\qquad\qquad gt​t=−1+2​M​rρ2,\displaystyle g_{tt}=-1+\frac{2Mr}{\rho^{2}}\;{,}
Δ=r2−2​M​r+a2,\displaystyle\Delta=r^{2}-2Mr+a^{2}\;, gt​φ=−2​M​r​a​sin2⁡θρ2,\displaystyle g_{t\varphi}=-\frac{2Mra\sin^{2}\theta}{\rho^{2}}\;{,}
gφ​φ=[r2+a2+2​M​r​a2​sin2⁡θρ2]​sin2⁡θ.\displaystyle g_{\varphi\varphi}=\big[r^{2}+a^{2}+\frac{2Mra^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}{\rho^{2}}\big]\sin^{2}\theta\;.

Here, aa and MM, which are required to satisfy 0<|a|<M0<|a|<M, are constants representing the angular momentum per unit mass and the mass of the black hole, respectively.

We now define r−<r+r_{-}<r_{+} to be the roots of Δ\Delta and fix a time orientation on the Lorentzian manifold (ℳ,g)(\mathcal{M},g) by stipulating that −∂r-\partial_{r} is future directed. The time oriented Lorentzian manifold (ℳ,g)(\mathcal{M},g) is called the interior of a subextremal Kerr black hole. Moreover, let us fix an orientation by stipulating that the Lorentzian volume form vol=ρ2​sin⁡θ​d​t∧d​r∧d​θ∧d​φ\mathrm{vol}=\rho^{2}\sin\theta\,dt\wedge dr\wedge d\theta\wedge{d}\varphi is positive.

For later reference we note that the inverse metric g−1g^{-1} in the Boyer–Lindquist coordinates (t,φ,r,θ)(t,\varphi,r,\theta) is given by

(2.2) g−1=(−gφ​φΔ​sin2⁡θgt​φΔ​sin2⁡θ00gt​φΔ​sin2⁡θ−gt​tΔ​sin2⁡θ0000Δρ200001ρ2).g^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}-\frac{g_{\varphi\varphi}}{\Delta\sin^{2}\theta}&\frac{g_{t\varphi}}{\Delta\sin^{2}\theta}&0&0\\ \frac{g_{t\varphi}}{\Delta\sin^{2}\theta}&-\frac{g_{tt}}{\Delta\sin^{2}\theta}&0&0\\ 0&0&\frac{\Delta}{\rho^{2}}&0\\ 0&0&0&\frac{1}{\rho^{2}}\end{pmatrix}\;.

Let r∗​(r)r^{*}(r) be a function on (r−,r+)(r_{-},r_{+}) satisfying d​r∗d​r=r2+a2Δ\frac{dr^{*}}{dr}=\frac{r^{2}+a^{2}}{\Delta} and r¯​(r)\overline{r}(r) a function on (r−,r+)(r_{-},r_{+}) satisfying d​r¯d​r=aΔ\frac{d\overline{r}}{dr}=\frac{a}{\Delta}. We now define the following functions on ℳ\mathcal{M}:

v+:=t+r∗\displaystyle v_{+}:=t+r^{*}\quad ,φ+:=φ+r¯,\displaystyle,\qquad\varphi_{+}:=\varphi+\overline{r}\;,
v−:=r∗−t\displaystyle v_{-}:=r^{*}-t\quad ,φ−:=φ−r¯.\displaystyle,\qquad\varphi_{-}:=\varphi-\overline{r}\;.

Here, to be precise, φ+\varphi_{+} and φ−\varphi_{-} are defined modulo 2​π2\pi. It is easy to check that (v+,φ+,r,θ)(v_{+},\varphi_{+},r,\theta) and (v−,φ−,r,θ)(v_{-},\varphi_{-},r,\theta) are coordinate systems for ℳ\mathcal{M}. The metric gg in these coordinates takes the following form:

g=gt​t​d​v+2+gt​φ​(d​v+⊗d​φ++d​φ+⊗d​v+)+gφ​φ​d​φ+2+(d​v+⊗d​r+d​r⊗d​v+)−a​sin2⁡θ⁡(d​r⊗d​φ++d​φ+⊗d​r)+ρ2​d​θ2=gt​t​d​v−2−gt​φ​(d​v−⊗d​φ−+d​φ−⊗d​v−)+gφ​φ​d​φ−2+(d​v−⊗d​r+d​r⊗d​v−)+a​sin2⁡θ⁡(d​r⊗d​φ−+d​φ−⊗d​r)+ρ2​d​θ2.\begin{split}g&=g_{tt}\,dv_{+}^{2}+g_{t\varphi}\,\big(dv_{+}\otimes d\varphi_{+}+d\varphi_{+}\otimes dv_{+}\big)+g_{\varphi\varphi}\,d\varphi^{2}_{+}+\big(dv_{+}\otimes dr+dr\otimes dv_{+}\big)\\[2.0pt] &\qquad-a\sin^{2}\theta\,\big(dr\otimes d\varphi_{+}+d\varphi_{+}\otimes dr\big)+\rho^{2}\,d\theta^{2}\\[7.0pt] &=g_{tt}\,dv_{-}^{2}-g_{t\varphi}\,\big(dv_{-}\otimes d\varphi_{-}+d\varphi_{-}\otimes dv_{-}\big)+g_{\varphi\varphi}\,d\varphi^{2}_{-}+\big(dv_{-}\otimes dr+dr\otimes dv_{-}\big)\\[2.0pt] &\qquad+a\sin^{2}\theta\,\big(dr\otimes d\varphi_{-}+d\varphi_{-}\otimes dr\big)+\rho^{2}\,d\theta^{2}\;.\end{split}

This shows that in each of the above coordinate systems the metric extends in fact analytically to all positive values of rr. We now attach the following boundaries to the manifold ℳ\mathcal{M}: using the coordinate chart (v+,φ+,r,θ)(v_{+},\varphi_{+},r,\theta) we attach the boundary ℝ×{r=r+}×𝕊2\mathbb{R}\times\{r=r_{+}\}\times\mathbb{S}^{2}, which we call the event horizon and denote with ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+}. Moreover, using the coordinate chart (v−,φ−,r,θ)(v_{-},\varphi_{-},r,\theta) we attach the boundary ℝ×{r=r−}×𝕊2\mathbb{R}\times\{r=r_{-}\}\times\mathbb{S}^{2}, which we call the Cauchy horizon and denote with 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+}. The resulting manifold with boundary2525 25 We note explicitly that with our convention, ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} only consists of one (future affine complete) null hypersurface and 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{C}\mathcal{H}^{+} also only consists of one (past affine complete) null hypersurface. In particular, the dotted lines in Figure 2 are not part of the ℳ¯\overline{\mathcal{M}}. is denoted with ℳ¯\overline{\mathcal{M}} and is depicted using a Penrose-style representation in Figure 2.

2.1 Hypersurfaces

Note that ⟨d​v+,d​v+⟩=⟨d​v−,d​v−⟩=a2​sin2⁡θρ2\langle dv_{+},dv_{+}\rangle=\langle dv_{-},dv_{-}\rangle=\frac{a^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}{\rho^{2}}, thus showing that for a>0a>0 the level sets of v+v_{+} and v−v_{-} are timelike hypersurfaces away from the axis.

We now define the functions f+:=v+−r+r+f^{+}:=v_{+}-r+r_{+} and f−:=v−−r+r−f^{-}:=v_{-}-r+r_{-}. An easy computation gives

For convenience we introduce the abbreviations S=sin⁡θ{S}=\sin\theta and C=cos⁡θ{C}=\cos\theta. Moreover, using the Boyer–Lindquist coordinates, we define

V=(r2+a2)∂t+a∂φ and W=∂φ+aS2∂t.V=(r^{2}+a^{2})\partial_{t}+a\partial_{\varphi}\qquad\textnormal{ and }\qquad W=\partial_{\varphi}+a{S}^{2}\partial_{t}\;.

The vector fields e3e_{3} and e4e_{4} are null and future directed and satisfy ⟨e3,e4⟩=−2\langle e_{3},e_{4}\rangle=-2. Let us denote the distribution spanned by e3e_{3} and e4e_{4} by Π\Pi and the to Π\Pi orthogonal distribution by Π⟂\Pi^{\perp}. The vector fields e1e_{1} and e2e_{2} are not defined on the axis, but where defined they form an orthonormal basis for Π⟂\Pi^{\perp}.

The importance of this property will become obvious in Section 4.2.

2.4 The wave equation and an energy estimate

Let ψ∈C∞​(M,ℝ)\psi\in C^{\infty}(M,\mathbb{R}). The wave equation on the Kerr interior is defined by

□g​ψ:=(g−1)μ​ν​∇μ​∇νψ=0,\Box_{g}\psi:={(g^{-1})}^{\mu\nu}\nabla_{{\mu}}\nabla_{\nu}\psi=0\;,

where ∇\nabla, as above, denotes the Levi–Civita connection on (ℳ,g)(\mathcal{M},g) and here, and below, repeated indices are summed over. We recall that the stress-energy tensor 𝕋⁡[ψ]\mathbb{T}[\psi] of ψ\psi is given by

𝕋​[ψ]μ​ν:=∂μψ​∂νψ−12​gμ​ν​g−1​(d​ψ,d​ψ)\mathbb{T}[\psi]_{\mu\nu}:=\partial_{\mu}\psi\partial_{\nu}\psi-\frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu}g^{-1}(d\psi,d\psi)

and satisfies ∇μ𝕋​[ψ]μ​ν=□g​ψ​∂νψ\nabla^{\mu}\mathbb{T}[\psi]_{\mu\nu}=\Box_{g}\psi\partial_{\nu}\psi. We also recall that the deformation tensor π​(Z)μ​ν\pi(Z)_{\mu\nu} of a vector field ZZ is given by

π​(Z)μ​ν=∇μZν+∇νZμ.\pi(Z)_{\mu\nu}=\nabla_{\mu}Z_{\nu}+\nabla_{\nu}{Z}_{\mu}.

For a compact region D⊆ℳ¯D\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{M}} with piecewise smooth boundary ∂D\partial D, which is oriented with respect to the outward pointing normal, Stokes’ theorem now yields

(2.9) ∫∂Dι𝕋⁡[ψ]​(Z,⋅)♯​vol=∫Dd⁡(ι𝕋⁡[ψ]​(Z,⋅)♯​vol)=∫D(𝕋​[ψ]μ​ν​∇μZν+□g​ψ​Z​ψ)​vol.\int\limits_{\partial D}\iota_{\mathbb{T}[\psi](Z,\cdot)^{\sharp}}\,\mathrm{vol}=\int\limits_{D}d\big(\iota_{\mathbb{T}[\psi](Z,\cdot)^{\sharp}}\,\mathrm{vol}\big)=\int\limits_{D}\Big(\mathbb{T}[\psi]_{\mu\nu}\nabla^{\mu}Z^{\nu}+\Box_{g}\psi Z\psi\Big)\,\mathrm{vol}\;.

We refer to (2.9) as the energy estimate with multiplier ZZ in the region DD.

3 The main theorem

Let

Tℋ+=∂t+ar+2+a2∂φT_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}=\partial_{t}+\frac{a}{r_{+}^{2}+a^{2}}\partial_{\varphi}

denote a Hawking vector field of the event horizon; Tℋ+T_{\mathcal{H}^{+}} is Killing and orthogonal to ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+}. Moreover, we denote with

(3.1) T𝒞​ℋ+=(r−2+a2)∂t+a∂φT_{\mathcal{CH}^{+}}=(r_{-}^{2}+a^{2})\,\partial_{t}+a\,\partial_{\varphi}

a Hawking vector field of the Cauchy horizon, which is Killing and orthogonal to 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+}. We now state our theorem precisely as follows:

Theorem 3.2.

Let ψ:ℳ∪ℋ+→ℝ\psi:\mathcal{M}\cup\mathcal{H}^{+}\to\mathbb{R} be a smooth solution of the wave equation □g​ψ=0\Box_{g}\psi=0. Assume that there exists q>0q>0, δ∈[0,1)\delta\in[0,1) and C>0C>0 such that

  1. i)

    for all V≥1{\mathrm{V}}\geq 1, the following upper bound holds on ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+}:

    ∫ℋ+∩{v+≥V}𝕋[ψ](N~,e~4)vol−r≤CV−q,\int\limits_{\mathcal{H}^{+}\cap\{v_{+}\geq{\mathrm{V}}\}}\mathbb{T}[\psi](\tilde{N},\tilde{e}_{4})\,\mathrm{vol}_{-r}{\leq C}{\mathrm{V}}^{-q}\;,

    where N~\tilde{N} is a future directed timelike vector field that satisfies [N~,Tℋ+]=0[\tilde{N},T_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}]=0 on ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+};

  2. ii)

    for all V≥1{\mathrm{V}}\geq 1, the following lower bound holds on ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+}:

    (3.3) V−(q+δ)≤C∫ℋ+∩{v+≥V}𝕋[ψ](T𝒞​ℋ+,e~4)vol−r;{\mathrm{V}}^{-(q+\delta)}{\leq C}\int\limits_{\mathcal{H}^{+}\cap\{v_{+}\geq{\mathrm{V}}\}}\mathbb{T}[\psi](T_{\mathcal{CH}^{+}},\tilde{e}_{4})\,\mathrm{vol}_{-r}{;}
  3. iii)

    the following upper bound holds for the second order energy2727 27 Recall the definition of Ωℋ+i\Omega_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}^{i} in (2.8). on ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+}:

    ∑i=13∫ℋ+∩{v+≥1}𝕋[Ωℋ+iψ](N~,e~4)vol−r≤C.\sum\limits_{i=1}^{3}\int\limits_{\mathcal{H}^{+}\cap\{{v_{+}}\geq 1\}}\mathbb{T}[\Omega_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}^{i}\psi](\tilde{N},\tilde{e}_{4})\,\mathrm{vol}_{-r}\leq C\;.

It then follows that for every u0∈ℝu_{0}\in\mathbb{R} there exists a sequence vk∈ℝv_{k}\in\mathbb{R} with vk→∞v_{k}\to\infty for k→∞k\to\infty such that the following holds:2828 28 Here, in the preceding and in the following, ♯\sharp denotes the isomorphism between one-forms and vector fields given by “raising the index with the inverse of the metric gg”.

(3.4) ∫Σ−u0∩{v+≥vk}𝕋[ψ](−Δe4,(−df−)♯)volf−≳(vk)−(q+δ),\int\limits_{\Sigma^{-}_{u_{0}}\cap\{{v_{+}}\geq v_{k}\}}\mathbb{T}[\psi]\big(-\Delta e_{4},(-df^{-})^{\sharp}\big)\,\mathrm{vol}_{f^{-}}\gtrsim(v_{k})^{-(q+\delta)}\;,

where the implicit constant is independent of vkv_{k}. In particular, (3.4) implies2929 29 The fact that (3.4) implies (3.5) will be proven explicitly in Remark 3.9 below. that for every u0∈ℝu_{0}\in\mathbb{R} we have

(3.5) ∫Σ−u0∩{v+≥1}𝕋[ψ](e4,(−df−)♯)volf−=∞.\int\limits_{\Sigma^{-}_{u_{0}}\cap\{v_{+}\geq 1\}}\mathbb{T}[\psi]\big(e_{4},(-df^{-})^{\sharp}\big)\,\mathrm{vol}_{f^{-}}=\infty\;.

Note that the right hand side of (3.3) is not manifestly non-negative, since T𝒞​ℋ+T_{\mathcal{CH}^{+}} is spacelike on the event horizon ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+}.

Remark 3.6 (Alternative formulation of Theorem 3.2).

Assumption 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁i​i)ii) in Theorem 3.2 can be replaced by

  1. ii’)

    The wave ψ\psi is axisymmetric (i.e., ∂φψ=0\partial_{\varphi}\psi=0 everywhere in ℳ¯\overline{\mathcal{M}}) and there exists a δ∈[0,1)\delta\in[0,1) and a sequence wk∈ℝw_{k}\in\mathbb{R} with wk→∞w_{k}\to\infty for k→∞k\to\infty such that

    (3.7) wk−(q+δ)≲∫ℋ+∩{v+≥wk}𝕋[ψ](T𝒞​ℋ+,e~4)vol−r.w_{k}^{-(q+\delta)}\lesssim\int\limits_{\mathcal{H}^{+}\cap\{v_{+}\geq w_{k}\}}\mathbb{T}[\psi](T_{\mathcal{CH}^{+}},\tilde{e}_{4})\,\mathrm{vol}_{-r}\;.

Remark 3.8 (Yet another formulation of Theorem 3.2).

Remark 3.11 (Blow up of non-degenerate energy).

Let Σ\Sigma be a smooth spacelike hypersurface that intersects the Cauchy horizon transversally. Suppose Σ\Sigma is given by a defining function f:ℳ¯→ℝf:\overline{\mathcal{M}}\to\mathbb{R} (i.e., Σ=f−1​(0)\Sigma=f^{-1}(0)) such that (−d​f)♯(-df)^{\sharp} is a future-directed timelike vector field. Define the non-degenerate energy by

∫Σ𝕋⁡(e3+e4,(−𝑑f)♯)​volf,\int_{\Sigma}\mathbb{T}(e_{3}+e_{4},(-df)^{\sharp})\,\mathrm{vol}_{f},

where the volume form volf\mathrm{vol}_{f} is defined such that vol=d​f∧volf\mathrm{vol}=df\wedge\mathrm{vol}_{f}. (3.5) implies3232 32 Notice that ∫Σ−u0∩{v+≥1}𝕋[ψ](e3,(−df−)♯)volf−>0.\int\limits_{\Sigma^{-}_{u_{0}}\cap\{v_{+}\geq 1\}}\mathbb{T}[\psi]\big(e_{3},(-df^{-})^{\sharp}\big)\,\mathrm{vol}_{f^{-}}>0\;. that the non-degenerate energy on Σu0−∩{v+≥1}\Sigma^{-}_{u_{0}}\cap\{v_{+}\geq 1\} is infinite for every u0∈ℝu_{0}\in\mathbb{R}.

Moreover, by proving energy estimates locally near the Cauchy horizon, it can be shown that the non-degenerate energy is infinite on any smooth spacelike hypersurface intersecting the Cauchy horizon transversally, as is claimed in Theorem 1.2.

Remark 3.12 (Constructing solutions to the wave equation which satisfy the assumptions of Theorem 3.2).

It is a standard fact that the linear wave equation is well-posed towards the future with smooth data imposed on the event horizon ℋ+∩{v+≥1}\mathcal{H}^{+}\cap\{v_{+}\geq 1\} and spacelike hypersurface Σ1+\Sigma^{+}_{1}. Since the equation is linear, the solution exists and remains smooth in {v+≥1}∩{r∈(r−,r+]}\{v_{+}\geq 1\}\cap\{r\in(r_{-},r_{+}]\}. Note that the data on ℋ+∩{v+≥1}\mathcal{H}^{+}\cap\{v_{+}\geq 1\} can be prescribed such that the assumptions 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁i)−i​i​i)i)-iii) of Theorem 3.2 are satisfied. Moreover, the proof of Theorem 3.2 will show that the theorem also holds if ψ\psi is only assumed to be a smooth solution in the smaller set {v+≥1}∩{r∈(r−,r+]}\{v_{+}\geq 1\}\cap\{r\in(r_{-},r_{+}]\}. Hence, there exists a large class of solutions to the wave equation in the interior of the Kerr black hole which are initially regular but have infinite non-degenerate energy near the Cauchy horizon.

4 Stability estimates

4.1 Integrated energy decay for first derivatives

The results of this section depend only on the first assumption of Theorem 3.2:

Assumption 4.1.

Let ψ:ℳ∪ℋ+→ℝ\psi:\mathcal{M}\cup\mathcal{H}^{+}\to\mathbb{R} be a smooth solution of the wave equation □g​ψ=0\Box_{g}\psi=0 and assume that there exists a q>0q>0 such that for all V≥1{\mathrm{V}}\geq 1

∫ℋ+∩{v+≥V}𝕋[ψ](N~,e~4)vol−r≲V−q,\int\limits_{\mathcal{H}^{+}\cap\{v_{+}\geq{\mathrm{V}}\}}\mathbb{T}[\psi](\tilde{N},\tilde{e}_{4})\,\mathrm{vol}_{-r}\lesssim{\mathrm{V}}^{-q}\;,

where N~\tilde{N} is a future directed timelike vector field that satisfies [N~,Tℋ+]=0[\tilde{N},T_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}]=0.

We prove:

Under Assumption 4.1 the following holds: Let σ>0\sigma>0 and V{\mathrm{V}} be large enough3333 33 This is just to ensure that fγσf_{\gamma_{\sigma}} is defined in the region {f+≥V}\{f^{+}\geq{\mathrm{V}}\}. Then for any α∈[0,1)\alpha\in{[}0,1) we have

for some rblue∈(r−,r+)r_{\mathrm{blue}}\in(r_{-},r_{+}).

Proposition 4.3.

Under Assumption 4.1 the following holds: Let α∈[0,1)\alpha\in{[}0,1) and u1∈ℝu_{1}\in\mathbb{R} There then exists a constant C>0C>0 such that

(4.4) ∫{r≤rblue}∩{f−≤u1}(1(−Δ)α[Δ2(e4ψ)2+(e3ψ)2]+((e2ψ)2+(e1ψ)2))vol≤C\int\limits_{\{r\leq r_{\mathrm{blue}}\}\cap\{f^{-}\leq u_{1}\}}{\Big(}\frac{1}{(-\Delta)^{\alpha}}\Big[\Delta^{2}{(e_{4}}\psi{)}^{2}+{(e_{3}}\psi{)}^{2}\Big]+\big({(e_{2}}\psi{)}^{2}+{(e_{1}}\psi{)}^{2}\big)\Big)\,\mathrm{vol}\leq C\;

for rblue∈(r−,r+)r_{\mathrm{blue}}\in(r_{-},r_{+}) as in Proposition 4.2.

We depict in Figure 3 the regions of spacetime under consideration. The darker shaded region depicts the region of integration in Proposition 4.2, which is to the future of ΣV+\Sigma^{+}_{V} and to the past of γσ\gamma_{\sigma}. This region is further divided into two: the future and past of {r=rb​l​u​e}\{r=r_{blue}\}, where the weights in the integrated energy decay estimates are different.3434 34 We remind the readers that for rb​l​u​e∈(r−,r+)r_{blue}\in(r_{-},r_{+}), e~4\tilde{e}_{4} and e~3\tilde{e}_{3} are the regular vector fields in the region to the past of {r=rb​l​u​e}\{r=r_{blue}\} while e4e_{4} and e3e_{3} are the regular vector fields to the future of {r=rb​l​u​e}\{r=r_{blue}\}. The proof of Propositions 4.2 and 4.3 will be carried out using the energy estimate (2.9) with appropriate choices of multipliers ZZ. We now explain how one estimates the third term in (4.25): First recall that the tilded frame field {e~3,e~4,e1,e2}\{\tilde{e}_{3},\tilde{e}_{4},e_{1},e_{2}\} is invariant under the flow of the Killing vector field Tℋ+T_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}. However, the orthonormal basis {e1,e2}\{e_{1},e_{2}\} of Π⟂\Pi^{\perp} is not smooth on the axis. We thus introduce in addition an orthonormal basis {e1′,e2′}\{e_{1}^{\prime},e_{2}^{\prime}\} of Π⟂\Pi^{\perp} which is smooth in a small neighbourhood of the axis and also invariant under the flow of Tℋ+T_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}.4242 42 Note that so far there was no need to introduce a frame that is also regular at the axis, since we only decomposed expressions involving d​ψd\psi, i.e., first derivatives of ψ\psi, with respect to a frame field involving e1e_{1} and e2e_{2}. Technically, in such computations one restricts the domain to the region under consideration with the axis deleted. After estimating and rearranging such expressions we always ended up with the expression (e1​ψ)2+(e2​ψ)2(e_{1}\psi)^{2}+(e_{2}\psi)^{2}, which is equal to (g|Π⟂)−1​(d​ψ,d​ψ)(g|_{\Pi^{\perp}})^{-1}(d\psi,d\psi) and thus extends smoothly to the axis. By continuity, the obtained estimate thus also holds on the axis. Now, however, we are about to decompose expressions involving ∇∇ψ\nabla\nabla\psi. Here, it is important that we decompose with respect to a regular frame near the axis, since for example the term e2​(e1​ψ)e_{2}(e_{1}\psi) is in general unbounded when approaching the axis.

We then split the domain of integration in the third term of (4.25) in two disjoint regions AA (disjoint of the axis) and A′A^{\prime} (containing the axis) such that e1e_{1} and e2e_{2} are smooth on A¯\overline{A} and e1′e_{1}^{\prime} and e2′e_{2}^{\prime} are smooth on A′¯\overline{A^{\prime}}. In the following we decompose E​r​rErr in region AA with respect to the frame {e~3,e~4,e1,e2}\{\tilde{e}_{3},\tilde{e}_{4},e_{1},e_{2}\} and in region A′A^{\prime} with respect to the frame {e~3,e~4,e1′,e2′}\{\tilde{e}_{3},\tilde{e}_{4},e_{1}^{\prime},e_{2}^{\prime}\}. To simplify the presentation, we will restrict ourselves in the following discussion to region AA. Region A′A^{\prime}, however, is dealt with completely analogously.

From the coordinate representations of Ωℋ+i\Omega^{i}_{\mathcal{H}^{+}} in (2.8) it is easy to see that these vector fields are invariant under the flow of the Killing vector field Tℋ+T_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}. Hence, the same holds for the deformation tensor π⁡(Ωℋ+i)\pi(\Omega^{i}_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}) and its covariant derivative. The invariance under the flow of Tℋ+T_{\mathcal{H}^{+}} implies that the coefficients of the deformation tensor and its covariant derivative, when expressed in terms of the tilded frame, are uniformly bounded in the region under consideration. We proceed by writing all contractions in the term E​r​rErr in terms of the tilded frame, e.g. π​(Ωℋ+i)μ​ν​∇μ​∇νψ=π​(Ωℋ+i)4~​4~​(e~4​e~4​ψ+∇e~4e~4​ψ+…)\pi(\Omega^{i}_{\mathcal{H}^{+}})^{\mu\nu}\nabla_{\mu}\nabla_{\nu}\psi=\pi(\Omega^{i}_{\mathcal{H}^{+}})^{\tilde{4}\tilde{4}}(\tilde{e}_{4}\tilde{e}_{4}\psi+\nabla_{\tilde{e}_{4}}\tilde{e}_{4}\psi+\ldots). Again by the invariance of the frame field under the flow of the Killing vector field Tℋ+T_{\mathcal{H}^{+}} vector fields of the form ∇e~4e~4\nabla_{\tilde{e}_{4}}\tilde{e}_{4} have uniformly bounded coefficients when expressed in the tilded frame. We conclude that in region AA the term E​r​rErr can be written as a sum of terms of the form h⋅e⁡(f​ψ)h\cdot e(f\psi) and h⋅e​ψh\cdot e\psi, where hh is a uniformly bounded function and ee and ff are members of the tilded frame field.

Using this structure, we can now estimate in region AA terms of the form (h⋅e​ψ)​(N​Ωℋ+i​ψ)(h\cdot e\psi)(N\Omega^{i}_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}\psi) in the third term of (4.25) by

(4.29) |(h⋅e​ψ)​(N​Ωℋ+i​ψ)|≤ε−1​h2​(e​ψ)2+ε​(N​Ωℋ+i​ψ)2.|(h\cdot e\psi)(N\Omega^{i}_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}\psi)|\leq\varepsilon^{-1}h^{2}(e\psi)^{2}+\varepsilon({N}\Omega^{i}_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}\psi)^{2}\;.

Choosing ε>0\varepsilon>0 small enough and recalling that NN is invariant under the flow of Tℋ+T_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}, the second term can be absorbed by the second term in (4.25). The first term in (4.29), after integration, is bounded by Proposition 4.2.

It thus remains to deal with terms of the form h⋅e⁡(f​ψ)h\cdot e(f\psi) in E​r​rErr. We again use Cauchy–Schwarz to estimate

|(h⋅e⁡(f​ψ))​(N​Ωℋ+i​ψ)|≤ε−1​h2​(e⁡(f​ψ))2+ε​(N​Ωℋ+i​ψ)2.|\big(h\cdot e(f\psi)\big)(N\Omega^{i}_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}\psi)|\leq\varepsilon^{-1}h^{2}\big(e(f\psi)\big)^{2}+\varepsilon({N}\Omega^{i}_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}\psi)^{2}\;.

Choosing ε>0\varepsilon>0 small enough, the second term can again be absorbed. Recalling (4.28), we now show that the first term can be controlled by ∑i=13𝕋⁡[Ωℋ+i​ψ]​(N,(d​r)♯)\sum_{i=1}^{3}\mathbb{T}[\Omega^{i}_{\mathcal{H}^{+}}\psi](N,(dr)^{\sharp}) (modulo first order terms which, after integration, can again be controlled by Proposition 4.2). Key to this improved integrated energy decay estimate is the following lemma, which is a Hardy inequality:

Lemma 4.35.

There exists r~∈(r−,rblue]\tilde{r}\in(r_{-},r_{\mathrm{blue}}] sufficiently close to r−r_{-} such that the following estimate holds for all smooth functions ϕ\phi on ℳ\mathcal{M}:

Setting h=1(−Δ)αh=\frac{1}{(-\Delta)^{\alpha}}, we compute
